title: Deaths in custody against public approval, 2004 to 2026: the ratio no one publishes, administration by administration
dek: The deadliest years in detention were under Bush, and the public never knew. The lowest approval before this year came under Biden, when the death rate was the lowest ever. For two decades approval tracked the border, not the morgue. In 2026 the lines finally point the same way, and the polls say what moved them.
body:
Two numbers describe every administration’s immigration enforcement, and they are almost never printed side by side. One is how many people died in its custody. The other is how many Americans approved of what it was doing. Since Immigration and Customs Enforcement began keeping a death list in fiscal 2004, 272 people had died in its detention by January 19 of this year, by the count of a study published in JAMA in April; add the deaths ICE has listed since and the total is past 290 [1][7]. Over the same 22 years, Gallup and others have asked, administration after administration, whether Americans approve of the president’s handling of immigration [3][4].

Put together, the two series say something uncomfortable about what the public has been judging. The deadliest year in detention, by rate, was fiscal 2004, when 28 people died among a daily population of about 22,000, and almost nobody outside the system knew [1][12]. The year the public turned hardest against a president’s immigration policy, before this one, was 2024, when the death rate in detention was near the lowest ever recorded [1][6]. For two decades approval tracked the border. It did not track the morgue. This year, for the first time, the two lines point the same way, and the polling is specific about why.

## The ledger, administration by administration

The JAMA study, by Sanjay Basu of the University of California, San Francisco, and colleagues at Johns Hopkins and Stanford, built the first consistent series: deaths from ICE’s own records, divided by the agency’s average daily population, giving a death rate per 100,000 person-years, the measure used for jails and prisons [1]. The Watch has set each period beside the polling of its time.

- **George W. Bush, fiscal 2004 to 2008.** 91 deaths among about 25,000 people detained on an average day: 72.8 per 100,000, the highest of any period, with the single worst year, 127.7, in 2004 [1]. Removals rose from 240,665 to 359,795 a year [2]. Approval of Bush on immigration ran from 34 percent in January 2005 to 22 percent in February 2008; Gallup noted that a majority had never approved since it began asking [3][30].
- **Barack Obama, 2009 to 2016.** 72 deaths, and the rate fell by more than half, to 30.2 in the first term and 23.6 in the second, as detention held near 33,000 a day [1]. This was the peak of removals: 432,334 in fiscal 2013, more than in any year before or since [2]. Approval ran from 29 percent in 2010 to 44 percent in his last summer, with the low of 31 percent in June 2014, the year of the Central American children at the border [34][33][4].
- **Donald Trump, 2017 to 2020.** 44 deaths, a rate of 27.8, with detention climbing to a then-record 50,165 a day in fiscal 2019 [1][8]. The pandemic year broke the pattern: 21 deaths in fiscal 2020 among a population cut to 33,724, a rate of 75.6, with infections, COVID among them, the cause of nearly a third of the period’s deaths [1][8]. Approval of his handling of immigration sat at 40 to 41 percent in Gallup’s readings of 2017 and 2018 [35][9].
- **Joe Biden, 2021 to 2024.** 24 deaths, the fewest of any administration, and the lowest rate ever recorded, 13.0 in fiscal 2023, as detention fell to 19,461 a day in 2021 before climbing back to 37,721 [1][8]. Removals collapsed to 59,011 in 2021 and recovered to 271,484 by 2024 [8]. Approval fell from 41 percent in his first summer to 28 percent in February 2024, the lowest Gallup has recorded for any president on the question [36][6].
- **Donald Trump, 2025 to now.** 23 deaths in fiscal 2025, 22 of them after January 20, and 36 in fiscal 2026 by ICE’s own list, the most in any year since the list began [1][7][10]. The rate: 47.5 in fiscal 2025, 88.9 in the first three and a half months of fiscal 2026, and, by The Watch’s estimate from the full-year count of 36 and an average population of roughly 64,000, somewhere near 55 for the whole of fiscal 2026 [1][7][11]. Approval of his handling of immigration began at 46 percent in February 2025 and has sat between 35 and 40 percent since last summer: Gallup had 35 in June and 37 in November 2025 before it stopped measuring presidential approval; in 2026 Reuters/Ipsos has had 38 to 39, Quinnipiac 38, AP-NORC 38 to 39, the Economist/YouGov 40 [37][32][31][13][14][15][16][17].

## The series, year by year

For readers who want the raw numbers rather than the periods, here is ICE’s own count of deaths in its custody by fiscal year, from the list it released covering 2004 to 2016, its announcements since, and the study’s tally for the current year [38][39][40][41][7].

- Deaths: 2004, 28 · 2005, 21 · 2006, 19 · 2007, 12 · 2008, 11 · 2009, 14 · 2010, 8 · 2011, 10 · 2012, 8 · 2013, 9 · 2014, 6 · 2015, 7 · 2016, 10 · 2017, 12 · 2018, 9 · 2019, 8 · 2020, 21 · 2021, 5 · 2022, 3 · 2023, 4 · 2024, 12 · 2025, 23 · 2026, 36 [38][39][40][41][10][7].
- People detained on an average day: 2004, 21,298 · 2009, 32,098 · 2012, 34,260 · 2018, 42,188 · 2019, 50,165 · 2020, 33,724 · 2021, 19,254 · 2022, 22,577 · 2023, 28,131 · 2024, 37,721 · 2026, roughly 64,000 by The Watch’s reading of the point-in-time counts, which ran from 59,762 in September 2025 to a record 70,766 in January and 65,765 in July [42][40][8][11].

One caution on the Trump first-term row: ICE’s announcements for fiscal 2017 to 2020 add to 50 deaths, while the JAMA study counts 44 for the same years; the study excludes deaths that occurred after custody had formally ended, which may account for the gap [1][39][40].

## What the public was actually judging

Read the approval numbers against the border and the pattern is obvious. Bush’s worst years, 2006 to 2008, were the years of the failed immigration bills and of returns at the border near a million a year [30][2]. Obama’s low, June 2014, was the summer unaccompanied children overwhelmed the Rio Grande Valley; Pew found 28 percent approving of his handling of that crisis in July [4][5]. Biden’s 28 percent came in February 2024, at the height of the border crisis that dominated that year’s campaign [6]. Gallup’s longest-running immigration question, whether immigration should be decreased, tells the same story from the other side: 55 percent said decrease in 2024, the highest since 2001, when the border was the issue; the figure fell to 30 percent in 2025 and 29 percent this June, the lowest Gallup has ever measured, once the border was quiet and the enforcement had moved inland [18].

None of those swings had anything to do with detention deaths, and for most of the period the public could not have known about them. ICE did not publish a list. The count that first reached the public, 107 deaths since 2003, came from The New York Times’ reporting in January 2010, after the fiscal 2004 peak had come and gone [12]. ICE’s public death-reporting page covers fiscal 2018 onward; the researchers who now compute the rates worked from Freedom of Information Act files for every year before that [1].

What changed in 2026 is that the public began judging enforcement, not immigration. The “gone too far” question did not exist in a usable form before this administration, and it now returns a majority from every pollster: 57 percent in Harvard CAPS/Harris at the end of January, 58 percent in Reuters/Ipsos the same week, 60 percent calling the administration “too harsh” in Quinnipiac, 65 percent in NPR/PBS/Marist, 62 percent in AP-NORC on agents in cities in February and 55 percent in July, 53 percent in Fox News’ September poll of registered voters, and about six in ten in the AP Voter Poll on Election Day [28][13][14][16][29][15][19][20]. ICE itself went from 44 percent favorable in Pew’s 2018 survey to 35 percent favorable and 56 unfavorable in October, though Pew cautions that the two surveys were run differently [21]. Within three weeks of the Minneapolis shootings, YouGov found more Americans in favor of abolishing the agency than opposed, 46 to 43 [22].

The timing is the tell. The record deaths in custody had been reported for months before January 2026; the American Immigration Council called fiscal 2025 the deadliest year since 2004 in October, and NPR reported in March that fiscal 2026 had already passed it [10][23]. The approval numbers barely moved on that news. They moved in the last week of January, after federal agents shot and killed two U.S. citizens, Renée Good and Alex Pretti, in Minneapolis: Reuters/Ipsos, Quinnipiac, Marist, YouGov and AP-NORC all recorded their lows for the administration in the three weeks after January 24 [13][14][16][29][22]. The public did not turn against the program because of who died inside it. It turned because of who died on the street, on video.

## Why the two series do not move together

Three things keep deaths and approval apart. The first is visibility: a death in a detention center in rural Georgia produces a two-page report 90 days later, if the rule is followed; a shooting in Minneapolis produces video the same hour [10][23]. The second is scale: the detained population is small, about one in 5,000 Americans even at its record, and most people have never met anyone who has been inside [11]. The third is that the people who die are the people the public had already decided about. Gallup has asked since 2016 whether Americans favor deporting everyone in the country illegally. Support was 32 percent in 2016, 37 in 2019, 47 in 2024, and fell back to 38 in 2025 and 39 this June, even as the administration did more of it than any before [32][18]. Support for the policy and tolerance for its costs are not the same measure, and the second has never been polled directly.

There is one more pattern worth stating plainly. The death rate in detention has risen in every year that detention grew quickly, under both parties: 2004, as the system doubled after ICE’s creation; 2020, when the pandemic reached crowded facilities; and 2025 and 2026, when the population rose by half in a year and passed 70,000 [1][11]. The JAMA authors found that cardiovascular disease was the leading named cause, infections second, suicide third, and that the median age at death was 45 [1]. Deaths in detention are, mostly, deaths of people who needed medical care and did not get it in time; a 2024 analysis of 52 deaths from 2017 to 2021 concluded most would likely have been prevented with adequate care [23]. Rapid expansion is when care is thinnest.

## How to read a death rate

Three numbers are in circulation and they are not measuring the same thing. The Department of Homeland Security says the death rate in custody is 0.009 percent of the detained population, “consistent with the past decade” [24]. The Cato Institute, in 2020, measured deaths against admissions: 11.8 per 100,000 people booked in during fiscal 2020 [25]. The JAMA study measured against person-years, the time people actually spent in custody: 75.6 per 100,000 for the same year [1]. The three are compatible; they divide the same deaths by different denominators. A person booked in and released within days counts fully in an admissions rate and barely at all in a person-years rate. As stays have lengthened, the gap between the measures has widened, which is why the agency’s figure and the physicians’ figure can both be accurate and point in opposite directions.

The baseline matters too. The Bureau of Justice Statistics put the death rate in local jails at 167 per 100,000 in 2019 and in state prisons at 330 [26][27]. ICE detention, at 37 per 100,000 over 22 years and perhaps 55 this year, is lower than either, and DHS says its standards “exceed those of most U.S. prisons” [1][24]. But detainees are, on paper, a healthier population than a prison’s: younger, screened at intake, and held for months rather than decades, so a prison’s rate is not the right expectation [1]. Jails, which hold people for weeks and lose 30 percent of them to suicide, are the closer comparison, and the 2026 rate is a third of the way to the jail rate [26].

And the list is not the whole count. ICE records a death only while custody is active; someone released in a hospital and dying the next day is not on it, and the JAMA authors flag that as a source of undercounting [1]. Deaths in Border Patrol custody are kept separately. Deaths during arrests, like that of Jose Castro-Rivera, 25, killed by a truck during an arrest this year, sit at the edge of the definition [23]. The people shot by federal agents in Minneapolis were never in custody at all [22]. ICE is required to publish a report on each death within 90 days; by March its public page was current only to early January, and Sens. Jon Ossoff and Raphael Warnock found that the 48-hour interim notice had been issued in 15 of 49 deaths since January 2025 [23][7].

## The ratio, if you insist on one

Divide each administration’s detention death rate by the share of Americans who approved of its immigration policy and you get a number with no meaning, but the shape of it is instructive. Bush: 72.8 per 100,000 over an approval of roughly 27 percent, a ratio near 2.7. Obama: about 27 over 36 percent, 0.75. Trump’s first term: 27.8 over 40 percent, 0.7. Biden: about 22 over 33 percent, 0.65. Trump’s second term: about 55 over 38 percent, 1.4, and climbing toward Bush’s [1][8][3][4][6][9][13]. The honest reading is that the Bush years were the deadliest in detention by a wide margin and the public never knew; that the Obama, first Trump and Biden years were, on this measure, indistinguishable from one another; and that the present administration is the first to run a death rate well above the modern norm in front of a public that is watching. What the public is watching, the polls say, is not the detention center. It is the street outside it.
